title: Sublimis Deus (1537)
hookLine: Pope Paul III declares Indigenous peoples free and rational, often ignored by colonists

cards: Some questions should never need asking. On the island of Hispaniola, on a Sunday in Advent, a Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbed into the pulpit and put one to the Spanish settlers in front of him.
Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Las Casas later wrote down the sermon, and how angry the congregation was.
Years afterward, the question reached Rome, and a pope answered it in writing. His letter is named by its first two words: Sublimis Deus.

teach.b: They mean the sublime God, the God on high. The letter opens not with the Americas but with God, who made people able to know him. Next, the lie it names.

teach.h: A LIE CALLED BY ITS NAME.
teach.b: Paul the Third writes that some, moved by the enemy of the human race, have claimed that the peoples of the West and South should be treated like dumb animals, unable to receive the faith, and used that claim to put them to work.

teach.h: FREE, AND OWNERS OF WHAT THEY HAVE.
teach.b: These peoples are truly human, able to understand and receive the faith, and they may not be deprived of their liberty or their property, even if they are outside the faith.

The faith is to be offered by preaching and the example of a good life, not by force. Underneath is a line the letter leans on: Jesus sending out his apostles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations."

teach.h: INK, AND THE GAP AFTER IT.
teach.b: All, the pope writes, without exception, because all are able to receive the faith. Last, the gap. A letter from Rome is ink.

In the colonies, men with land and gold had every reason to look away, and on the ground the bull's promises were resisted and often not kept. Las Casas and others kept pressing its point before royal councils.
So Sublimis Deus is two things at once: a clear statement of what the Church said about human dignity, and a reminder that saying it is never the end of the work.

how: Catholics point to Sublimis Deus in Church teaching on human dignity; Indigenous Catholics and their bishops have cited it, alongside later papal apologies, when speaking about the history of the Americas.

o: a pope's letter calling the Americas' peoples truly human
a Latin hymn sung at Mass on the feast of Pentecost
a council's decree on preaching in the Americas

p: offered by preaching and good example

s: the letter says these peoples may keep their liberty and property even outside the faith
even if they are outside the faith, they may not be deprived of either.
once the pope wrote it, the colonists obeyed

the letter is named by its opening words

games.q: you're Paul III. some claim the peoples of the Americas are like animals, unable to receive the faith, and so may be put to forced labor. what do you write?
o: that they are truly human, free, and owners of their property.
that the question should be left to the colonists.
that they may be enslaved until they are baptized.
games.why: he declared them truly human and able to receive the faith, not to be deprived of liberty or property, and to be invited by preaching and good example.

practice: Bring to mind the Indigenous peoples of the land where you are right now, by name if you know it, or simply as the people who were here first. Think of them now, not only long ago: families, languages, elders, children.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words, or rest with the line the pope leaned on, all nations, without exception; if you don't, let them stay in your attention, as real as your own neighbors.

wordCard.voice: Sublimis Deus. The sublime God. A papal letter of Paul the Third declaring that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, free, and not to be enslaved. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the sublime God, the God on high; the letter's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: they are truly human. Ink first, then the long work after. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

sources.q: Going therefore, teach ye all nations.
